raw_case_text:
We describe the case of a 65-year-old woman who experienced a 2-week course of gradually worsened unilateral headaches and anorexia. She presented to our hospital with an episode of loss of consciousness and newly onset convulsive seizure. Thirteen years prior, she presented with primary complaints of headaches and gait disturbances. She was diagnosed with relapsing/remitting MS based on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which initially revealed periventricular and juxtacortical T2 hyperintense lesions (Fig. 1), followed by new right cerebral peduncle and left middle cerebellar peduncle lesions (3 months later). Oligoclonal bands were absent from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
Twelve years ago, she started taking fingolimod as a disease-modifying treatment (DMT) for MS. Among the limited treatment options available at the time (i.e. interferon beta-1a/1b and fingolimod), fingolimod was chosen over interferon beta because a) she had a history of depression, for which interferon beta is contraindicated due to possible exacerbation of depressive symptoms, and b) several factors including brain stem lesions and short interval between relapses suggested an active disease calling for higher efficacy therapy.
After the introduction of fingolimod, the patient has been clinically stable with mild disability at the Kurtzke Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score 1, without evidence of recurrence or progressive atrophy on brain MRI. Peripheral blood lymphocyte count remained at 400-600/microL, slightly below the reference range, a common side effect of fingolimod, but never below 200/microL, a criterion for discontinuing the drug. Because she was clinically stable, fingolimod was continued for 12 years without switching to other DMTs.
On examination upon this admission, she was afebrile. Laboratory tests revealed mild peripheral lymphopenia (520/uL). Head CT and brain MRI with and without gadolinium contrast enhancement showed no new lesions nor meningeal enhancement (Fig. 2). Seizure was refractory to levetiracetam and fosphenytoin. Progressive headache and refractory seizure suggested a possible central nervous system infection. A CSF examination performed two days after hospitalization revealed an opening pressure of 14 cm H2O, a cell count of 15/microL (80 % mononuclear cells), 52 mg/dL protein, and 62 mg/dL glucose (174 mg/dL blood glucose).
The CSF was positive for cryptococcal antigen (1:1024). Multiplex polymerase chain reaction (BioFire  FilmArray  Meningitis/Encephalitis Panel) was positive for Cryptococcus; it was finally identified as C. neoformans using CSF culture. CSF myelin basic protein levels were marginally elevated at 111.5 pg/mL (reference: < 102 pg/mL); however, the IgG index remained within normal limits at 0.672 (reference: < 0.73). Adenosine deaminase (ADA) levels were within the normal range at 4.2 IU/L, and both Treponema pallidum antibody and oligoclonal bands were negative. Blood was also positive for cryptococcal antigen (1:1024); however, blood cultures were negative. Cryptococcal meningitis was diagnosed. Induction therapy with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously once daily) and flucytosine (25 mg/kg orally, four times a day) was started on hospital day 2. Her headaches subsided within a few days.
On hospital day 5, antiseizure medications were switched from intravenous to oral drugs, comprising levetiracetam, lacosamide and clobazam, and no recurrence of seizure was observed.
Four days after treatment initiation, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) concentrations increased to 158 U/L (reference range, 8-38) and 364 U/L (reference range, 4-44), respectively, and drug-induced liver injury was suspected. Considering the importance of treating cryptococcal meningitis, liposomal amphotericin B was continued as a key drug. Flucytosine and the antiepileptic drug, clobazam, which was more likely to cause liver dysfunction than levetiracetam and lacosamide (which were administered simultaneously), were discontinued. The AST and ALT concentrations gradually improved to 25 U/L and 42 U/L, respectively, over the 2 weeks after drug discontinuation. A follow-up CSF examination was performed 1 week and 2 weeks after treatment. C. neoformans was still positive in the first follow-up CSF culture; however, the CSF culture was negative 2 weeks after treatment. In general, fluconazole is proposed to add to liposomal amphotericin B as the induction treatment for cryptococcal meningitis in the absence of flucytosine. However, concerns arose regarding the addition of a new drug in the presence of liver dysfunction; therefore, we decided to continue treatment with liposomal amphotericin B alone.
Liposomal amphotericin B was continued for 4 weeks after a negative CSF culture (a total of 6 weeks; liver function improved in this time), followed by fluconazole (400 mg orally once daily) for 8 weeks as consolidation therapy, and fluconazole (200 mg orally once daily) for 1 year as maintenance therapy. She was treated for seizures with intravenous levetiracetam and fosphenytoin immediately after hospitalization, and after 5 days, treatment was switched to oral levetiracetam and lacosamide (oral clobazam was also started, but discontinued due to liver dysfunction, as described above). There was no recurrence of seizures. To treat MS, fingolimod was discontinued and replaced with an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, ofatumumab, because of its reliable efficacy and safety.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis presented with a 2-week course of gradually worsening unilateral headaches and anorexia followed by acute loss of consciousness and a new-onset convulsive seizure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 weeks prior to admission, the patient experienced progressively worsening unilateral headaches and anorexia, culminating in an episode of loss of consciousness and a first-time convulsive seizure prompting hospitalization. She had been on continuous fingolimod therapy for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis for the preceding 12 years.
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (diagnosed 13 years prior; EDSS score 1) treated with fingolimod for 12 years (chronic mild lymphopenia 400-600/uL); history of depression.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for unilateral headache, anorexia, loss of consciousness, and convulsive seizure. Home medication: fingolimod.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile on admission; presented with convulsive seizure activity refractory to initial IV levetiracetam and fosphenytoin.
objective.routine_investigations: Mild peripheral lymphopenia (520/uL). Serum cryptococcal antigen was positive (1:1024), while blood cultures were negative. Four days after starting treatment, AST and ALT rose to 158 U/L (reference: 8-38) and 364 U/L (reference: 4-44), respectively.
objective.advanced_workup: Head CT and brain MRI with and without gadolinium showed stable chronic MS lesions with no new parenchymal lesions or meningeal enhancement. Hospital day 2 lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 14 cmH2O, cell count 15/uL (80% mononuclear cells), protein 52 mg/dL, glucose 62 mg/dL (blood glucose 174 mg/dL), marginally elevated myelin basic protein 111.5 pg/mL (reference: <102 pg/mL), normal IgG index 0.672 (reference: <0.73), normal ADA 4.2 IU/L, and negative Treponema pallidum antibody and oligoclonal bands.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of fingolimod-associated Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis presenting with new-onset refractory seizures, confirmed by CSF and serum cryptococcal antigen titers of 1:1024, positive BioFire FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis PCR panel for Cryptococcus, and CSF fungal culture isolating C. neoformans. Induction therapy with IV liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg/day) and oral flucytosine (25 mg/kg four times daily) was started on day 2; due to drug-induced liver injury on day 6 (AST 158 U/L, ALT 364 U/L), flucytosine and clobazam were discontinued and liposomal amphotericin B monotherapy was continued for 6 weeks total (4 weeks after CSF culture sterilization at week 2), followed by oral fluconazole consolidation (400 mg/day for 8 weeks) and maintenance (200 mg/day for 1 year). Seizures were controlled with oral levetiracetam and lacosamide, and fingolimod was switched to ofatumumab without recurrence.
